reference.source: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Erectile dysfunction is the persistent inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual activity, and it is common with increasing age
Causes are broadly organic (vascular, neurogenic, hormonal, anatomical, drug-induced) or psychogenic, and the two frequently coexist
Vascular disease is the leading organic cause, so ED often shares risk factors with, and can be an early warning sign of, cardiovascular disease and diabetes
A history distinguishing gradual organic onset from sudden situational psychogenic ED is key; preserved spontaneous nocturnal or early-morning erections point toward a psychogenic cause
Assessment should review medications (antihypertensives, antidepressants, antiandrogens), lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol, obesity), and endocrine and psychological status
First-line pharmacological management is with phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, alongside optimisation of cardiovascular risk factors and lifestyle modification
PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrate therapy because of the risk of profound hypotension
Second-line options include intracavernosal or intraurethral vasoactive agents and vacuum devices, with penile prosthesis implantation reserved for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Penile erection depends on neurally mediated relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle, increased arterial inflow, and veno-occlusion that traps blood within the corpora cavernosa; nitric oxide and the cyclic GMP pathway are central to this process. Erectile dysfunction arises when any of these mechanisms fails: arterial insufficiency from atherosclerosis reduces inflow, veno-occlusive dysfunction allows leak, neuropathy (for example from diabetes or pelvic surgery) impairs signalling, and hormonal deficiency (notably hypogonadism) reduces desire and erectile capacity. Psychogenic factors act through central inhibition of the erectile response. Many patients have a mixed, multifactorial aetiology.
additionalDifferentials: Neurogenic causes (diabetic neuropathy, pelvic surgery, spinal cord disease)
additionalInvestigations: Fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipid profile to assess cardiovascular and metabolic risk
Morning serum testosterone, with prolactin and other hormones if deficiency is suspected
Blood pressure and cardiovascular risk assessment
Validated questionnaires such as the International Index of Erectile Function
Penile Doppler ultrasound and specialist vascular studies in selected complex or younger patients
redFlags: ED as a sentinel marker of undiagnosed cardiovascular disease or diabetes
Erectile dysfunction with neurological signs suggesting spinal cord or cauda equina pathology
Concurrent nitrate use, which contraindicates PDE5 inhibitors
Features suggesting a pituitary lesion (hyperprolactinaemia, visual field changes) requiring endocrine evaluation
reference.prognosis: Erectile dysfunction is highly treatable in most men, with many responding to PDE5 inhibitors and risk-factor modification; prognosis depends on the underlying cause, and it should prompt evaluation and management of associated cardiovascular risk.
pitfalls: Prescribing PDE5 inhibitors to a patient taking nitrates
Treating ED symptomatically without addressing underlying cardiovascular or metabolic disease
Overlooking hypogonadism or hyperprolactinaemia as reversible causes
Failing to consider medication side effects as a contributor
Neglecting the psychological and relationship dimensions of the problem
management: Lifestyle modification with smoking cessation, weight reduction, regular exercise and moderation of alcohol, alongside optimisation of cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors
Review of contributing medications such as antihypertensives, antidepressants and antiandrogens, substituting where feasible
First-line pharmacological treatment with phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors
Testosterone replacement where hypogonadism is confirmed biochemically
Psychosexual counselling and cognitive behavioural approaches where a psychogenic component is prominent
Second-line therapy with intracavernosal or intraurethral alprostadil, or a vacuum erection device, when oral agents fail
Penile prosthesis implantation for refractory disease unresponsive to other measures
Cardiovascular risk assessment and referral, as erectile dysfunction may be an early marker of occult vascular disease
